problems.title: Constant-stretch distances with polylogarithmic update and query time
problems.question: Can constant-stretch distance values on always-expanders be maintained with polylogarithmic update and query time, improving the known O(n^α)-update frontier for every fixed α>0?
problems.origin: Sharpened here from the distance-oracle frontier [HLS24] and expander-specific limitations [HPS22]. The exact target is not a quoted conjecture.
problems.significance: This asks whether expansion removes a substantial part of the cost of dynamic distances. Connectivity and logarithmic diameter are already guaranteed; estimating a short distance still requires information that a diameter bound does not provide. A fixed stretch is essential for a meaningful separation from generic subpolynomial tradeoffs.
problems.formulation:
Gₜ is a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Every edge insertion or deletion preserves maximum degree Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ)≥φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀,φ₀. The class has no planar restriction; expansion is promised, not certified by the data structure.

Φ(G)=min∅≠S⊊V |∂S| / min{vol(S),vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈Sdeg(v).
distₜ(a,b) ≤ d̂ₜ(a,b) ≤ C·distₜ(a,b),   C>1 independent of n.

Seek a deterministic data structure with P=n^(1+o(1)), S=n^(1+o(1)) words, amortized U=polylog n and worst-case Q=polylog n. The quantifier is “there exists a fixed C”; C is not an input approximation parameter. Queries return one distance estimate, not a path. Guarantees must hold over every polynomial-length legal sequence, including adaptive updates. A sharper near-linear P,S bound is a separate strengthening.
problems.known: For every fixed α>0, [HLS24] supplies the numerical frontier below. Setting α to shrink with n changes the stretch; it does not give a fixed-C polylogarithmic-update theorem. Exact-distance hardness in [HPS22] cannot be transferred to this approximation target without a gap argument.
problems.verification: B · Sharpened candidate. The checked upper bounds do not supply this combination of stretch, space and operation times. The expander lower bound [HPS22] is for exact distance. A proof that the proposed approximation target is open is not claimed.
comments: All vertices must remain queryable; maintaining only an expander core changes the question.
Single-edge updates and degree bounds are compatible; requiring exact d-regularity after every single insertion/deletion would make the model degenerate.
The contribution class describes the theorem sought, not a prediction of difficulty or acceptance.
literature: For exact expander distances, Theorem 36 excludes simultaneous U=O(n^(1/2−δ)), Q=O(n^(1−δ)) under OMv. Matching statements have different promises; this is not an approximate-distance lower bound.
Theorem 1.3: P=O(m₀^(1+α)), U=O(n^α) worst-case, Q=O(α⁻⁴ log log n), stretch 2^poly(1/α); deterministic. Fixed α gives constant stretch.
The almost-linear regime has total update time m^(1+o(1)) and approximation n^o(1); these are not polylogarithmic update time and fixed constant stretch.
For 512≤k≤(log n)^(1/49), 1/k≤δ≤1/400: size n^(1+O(1/k)), update n^O(δ), recourse n^O(1/k), stretch poly(k)·2^O(1/δ⁶). A maintained spanner does not automatically answer path queries.

audit.decision: Retained with a quantified frontier and explicit quantifiers.
audit.gap: Replace polynomial n^α update dependence by polylog n while keeping C independent of n; retain fast arbitrary-pair queries.
audit.caution: This is the strongest directly applicable tradeoff verified in the audit, not a claim of a uniquely optimal running time. P, S, stretch and U cannot be minimized independently.

bounds.scope: Deterministic, any fixed α>0; applies to this graph class. The theorem does not separately state a space bound, so no near-linear-space claim is inferred.
bounds.locator: Theorem 1.3 (PDF p. 4); parameter ε renamed α

bounds.scope: Maintain bounded-degree adjacency and run BFS per query. This meets the class/output requirements but not the target Q.

problems.title: Polylogarithmic updates for logarithmic-length path reporting
problems.question: Can every pair in an always-expander be joined by an explicitly reported O(log n)-edge path using polylogarithmic update time?
problems.origin: A fully dynamic all-vertex path interface, compared directly with [HLS24] and the decremental expander interface in [CH23].
problems.significance: A short-path data structure supports routing even when multiplicative distance approximation is unnecessary. The required output is a usable path in the current graph. This is a distinct target from a distance estimate: the guarantee is absolute length, including for nearby endpoints.
problems.formulation:
Gₜ is a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Every edge insertion or deletion preserves maximum degree Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ)≥φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀,φ₀. The class has no planar restriction; expansion is promised, not certified by the data structure.

Φ(G)=min∅≠S⊊V |∂S| / min{vol(S),vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈Sdeg(v).

After each update, query(a,b) must return a simple a–b path P contained in the current graph, with |P|≤K log n for a constant K depending only on Δ₀,φ₀ and the algorithm. All vertices are supported; there is no pruned or unsupported set.

Pinit, S = n^(1+o(1));   U=polylog n amortized;   Q=polylog n+O(|P|).

Require determinism and arbitrary polynomial-length legal sequences. The path is charged edge by edge. This asks for absolute length, not constant stretch relative to dist(a,b).
problems.known: [HLS24] already gives U=O(n^α) for each fixed α>0, with reported walk length O(Cα log n) and O(log n) query time on this unweighted class. Erasing loops takes O(log n), so a simple path follows. The remaining issue is the polylogarithmic update bound with an n-independent length factor. A source supplying only a spanner is not yet a pair-path oracle.
problems.verification: The audit replaces the previous weak baseline with the directly applicable HLS24 theorem. The short-cycle connection is recorded as an unproved implication, not as a conditional lower bound. The contribution label is changed to Major because the target improves a general n^α frontier while maintaining a strict path-length bound.
comments: No formal “short-cycle hard” classification is asserted. Turning a pair-path oracle into a cycle decomposition needs a reduction that charges all work, bounds uncovered edges, and preserves the oracle’s expansion promise after deletions.
The published short-cycle algorithms concern arbitrary static graphs and multiple edge-disjoint cycles. Finding one short path is a different interface.
A decremental truncated BFS tree has O(m log n) total work under a permanent diameter bound. Mixed insertions/deletions invalidate that monotone-distance argument.
literature: Deterministic P=O(n^(1+α)), U=O(n^α), distance Q=O(α⁻⁴ log log n); a reported walk costs Q+O(|P|). For fixed α, expansion makes |P|=O(log n).
Decremental total time m^(1+O(ε))Δ⁵/φ²; path length 2^O(1/ε⁶)Δ² log n/φ, reporting linear in length. Deletion budget nφ²/(2¹³Δ⁴), with excluded vertices.
Deterministic m^(1+o(1)) time for O(log² n)-length cycles with O(n log n) uncovered edges; another tradeoff gives Õ(m) time, O(log n) cycles, n^(1+o(1)) uncovered edges.
Historical m^(1+o(1)) algorithm with cycle length n^o(1) and n^(1+o(1)) uncovered edges. These three parameters are distinct from single-path reporting.

audit.decision: Reframed; no unsupported hardness label.
audit.gap: Improve U=O(n^α), available for any fixed α>0, to polylog n without letting the path-length factor grow with n.
audit.caution: A formal reduction to a named conjecture was not verified. The current frontier is an upper-bound comparison, not a proof of hardness.

bounds.label: Fully dynamic, all queried pairs
bounds.runtime: P=O(n^(1+α)); U=O(n^α) worst-case; Q=O(log n); |P|=O(Cα log n).
bounds.scope: Deterministic; fixed α>0. Loop erasure is linear because the input is unweighted and the entire reported walk is short.

bounds.label: Simple near-linear-space alternative
bounds.runtime: P,S=O(n); U=O(n); Q=O(log n); |P|=O(log n).
bounds.scope: Rebuild a BFS tree after each update; join the queried vertices in the tree.

problems.title: A constant approximation gap in expander distance lower bounds
problems.question: Does a fixed approximation factor greater than one retain an OMv-based dynamic distance barrier on always-expanders?
problems.origin: A hardness question extracted from the exact-versus-approximate distinction in [HPS22].
problems.significance: An exact lower bound may rely on an additive difference that becomes negligible after expanding the graph. A constant-gap lower bound would say which approximation guarantees are genuinely blocked by expansion-preserving hardness, rather than merely importing hardness from general graphs.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(V,Eₜ) be a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Each operation inserts or deletes one edge. Every resulting graph satisfies max degree ≤ Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ) ≥ φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀, φ₀. The input is not restricted to planar graphs. Vertices need not remain regular.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).
dist(a,b) ≤ d̂(a,b) ≤ (1+η)dist(a,b), with a fixed η>0 independent of n.

Concrete target: find a fixed η for which, under OMv, no data structure with polynomial preprocessing has both U=O(n1/2−δ) and Q=O(n1−δ) for any fixed δ>0. For definiteness, target deterministic data structures, amortized update and worst-case query time, and polynomial preprocessing. The reduction must keep every intermediate graph inside the promise class.
problems.known: [HPS22] establishes the indicated exponent barrier for exact distances on constant-degree bipartite expanders. Its approximation lower bounds elsewhere in the paper must not be conflated with that expander theorem.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Downgraded: the required approximation gap has not been established.

Not a source-explicit conjecture. Before treating it as a paper topic, the approximation gap of the reduction needs an independent audit.
comments: An inverse-polynomial relative gap is insufficient: η must be a positive constant.
A reduction that first removes an expander backbone and later restores it violates the dynamic promise.
This question concerns a restricted near-exact approximation factor; it would not by itself rule out every larger fixed stretch.
literature: For exact expander distances, Theorem 36 excludes simultaneous U=O(n^(1/2−δ)), Q=O(n^(1−δ)) under OMv. Matching statements have different promises; this is not an approximate-distance lower bound.
Theorem 1.3: P=O(m₀^(1+α)), U=O(n^α) worst-case, Q=O(α⁻⁴ log log n), stretch 2^poly(1/α); deterministic. Fixed α gives constant stretch.

audit.decision: Downgraded: the required approximation gap has not been established.
audit.gap: Prove or refute the stated fixed-η OMv barrier; the exact theorem alone is insufficient.
audit.caution: Not a source-explicit conjecture. Before treating it as a paper topic, the approximation gap of the reduction needs an independent audit.

bounds.label: Verified conditional barrier
bounds.runtime: Exact distances: no simultaneous U=O(n^(1/2−δ)), Q=O(n^(1−δ)) under OMv.
bounds.scope: Constant-degree bipartite expanders. This is an exact-distance statement.

bounds.label: Closest quantified fully dynamic frontier
bounds.runtime: P=O(n^(1+α)); U=O(n^α) worst-case; Q=O(α⁻⁴ log log n); stretch Cα=2^poly(1/α).
bounds.scope: Deterministic, any fixed α>0; applies to this graph class. The theorem does not separately state a space bound, so no near-linear-space claim is inferred.
bounds.locator: Theorem 1.3 (PDF p. 4); parameter ε renamed α

problems.title: Maintain a Schur complement on √n fixed terminals with small recourse
problems.question: Can a fully dynamic always-expander maintain an explicit spectral Schur complement sparsifier on √n prescribed terminals in Õ(√n) update time and polylogarithmic recourse?
problems.origin: A terminal sparsification question motivated by [DGGP19], [CGHPS20] and the improved dynamic primitive [BGJLLPS22].
problems.significance: A small terminal graph preserves all terminal electrical energies and resistances. Low recourse matters when another dynamic algorithm consumes its edge changes: a cheap internal update that rewrites the whole terminal graph can still be expensive to use.
problems.formulation:
Gₜ is a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Every edge insertion or deletion preserves maximum degree Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ)≥φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀,φ₀. The class has no planar restriction; expansion is promised, not certified by the data structure.

Φ(G)=min∅≠S⊊V |∂S| / min{vol(S),vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈Sdeg(v).

A prescribed set T⊂V of k=⌈√n⌉ vertices is fixed before preprocessing; F=V∖T. Fix ε∈(0,1/10). Maintain a nonnegatively weighted graph Hₜ on exactly T, with Õ(kε⁻²) edges, such that

Sₜ=Lₜ[T,T]−Lₜ[T,F]Lₜ[F,F]⁻¹Lₜ[F,T];   (1−ε)Sₜ ≼ L(Hₜ) ≼ (1+ε)Sₜ.

Target: P,S=Õ(n·poly(1/ε)), expected amortized U=Õ(√n·poly(1/ε)), and expected amortized recourse R=polylog n·poly(1/ε). Recourse counts each inserted/deleted edge and each weight change in the explicit Hₜ, including all changes during rebuilding. The update returns this edit list; enumerating Hₜ costs Õ(kε⁻²). Require high-probability spectral validity throughout any polynomial-length oblivious update sequence. No extra terminals may be introduced in the output.
problems.known: Static construction already takes Õ(m+nε⁻²) time with Õ(kε⁻²) output edges [DKPPRS17]. The dynamic primitives below permit terminal growth; their cheap terminal-to-terminal updates must be charged together with promotions and rebuilding. Neither pairwise resistance sketches nor separator-based algorithms establish this fixed-terminal, explicit-recourse interface.
problems.verification: Reframed after checking the 2019, 2020 and 2022 dynamic sparsifier primitives. For β=n⁻¹ᐟ² and m=Θ(n), the 2022 initialization is Õ(n²ε⁻²), AddTerminal is Õ(nε⁻²), and materializing SC is Õ(√nε⁻²). Charging initialization over a √n-operation epoch alone costs Õ(n³ᐟ²ε⁻²) per operation. These are substitutions into that theorem, not asserted lower bounds; the static rebuild baseline is better for our fixed-T comparison.
comments: A weight modification counts as recourse even if the endpoints of an output edge stay unchanged. An implicit dense rank-one update is not one edit in this interface.
The requirement “exactly T” is deliberate. Allowing a maintained superset T⊆C with |C|=O(√n) is a distinct relaxation and should have its own theorem statement.
At constant ε, rebuilding the static sparsifier gives U=Õ(n) and R=Õ(√n). The question requires improvements in both quantities, with every rebuild charged.
The former high-precision resistance-index question has been replaced here. Fast scalar resistance estimates and dynamic terminal sparsification have different output guarantees.
literature: Static prescribed-terminal approximate Schur complement: Õ(m+nε⁻²) construction, O(kε⁻² log(n/δ)) output entries, success ≥1−δ.
Lemma 1.1; terminal augmentation and operation budget
Unweighted initialization Õ(mβ⁻²ε⁻⁴), O(βm)-operation epoch, augmented terminal set of size O(βm). An epoch primitive is not an indefinite fixed-terminal data structure.
Weighted SC primitive: initialization Õ(mβ⁻⁴ε⁻⁴), update Õ(β⁻²ε⁻²), O(βm) operations; total edge changes Õ(mβ⁻¹ε⁻²). Recourse and rebuilds enter the hierarchy explicitly.
Improved initialization Õ(mβ⁻²ε⁻²); AddTerminal Õ(β⁻²ε⁻²); updates with both endpoints terminal Õ(1); SC output Õ(βmε⁻²). Terminals grow, with oblivious updates. Requires β<ε².

audit.decision: Replaced the resistance-value target with a precise fixed-terminal recourse target.
audit.gap: At constant ε, improve static rebuilding from (U,R)=(Õ(n),Õ(√n)) to (Õ(√n),polylog n).
audit.caution: Small-terminal dynamic SC work is substantial prior art. Fixed versus augmented terminals, output edits and initialization amortization are essential novelty checks.

bounds.label: Matching output; static rebuild after every update
bounds.runtime: P=Õ(nε⁻²); U=Õ(nε⁻²); output size and R=Õ(√nε⁻²).
bounds.scope: Prescribed fixed T; randomized with failure probability reduced for the entire horizon. Storage of the input and construction workspace is counted separately from output size.

bounds.label: Related dynamic primitive at β=n⁻¹ᐟ²
bounds.runtime: P=Õ(n²ε⁻²); promotion=Õ(nε⁻²); terminal-edge update=Õ(1); output=Õ(√nε⁻²).
bounds.scope: Terminals are selected/augmented by the algorithm; arbitrary updated endpoints must first be promoted. Thus this row does not meet the fixed-T contract. The theorem requires β<ε², hence n⁻¹ᐟ²<ε² in this substitution (in particular, fixed ε and sufficiently large n).

problems.title: Find energy-heavy edges of an implicitly changing electrical flow
problems.question: Can a dynamic always-expander locate all electrically important edges without materializing the changing potential vector?
problems.origin: An implicit-flow reporting interface compared with dynamic Laplacian and locator primitives in [DGGP19] and [BGJLLPS22].
problems.significance: An algorithm often needs the identities of the few edges carrying substantial energy, not just the total energy or a value at a named coordinate. Requiring the data structure to discover those edges makes the output task different from pointwise resistance or voltage estimation.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(V,Eₜ) be a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Each operation inserts or deletes one edge. Every resulting graph satisfies max degree ≤ Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ) ≥ φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀, φ₀. The input is not restricted to planar graphs. Vertices need not remain regular.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).

Orient edges arbitrarily; Bₜ is the vertex-by-edge incidence matrix and Lₜ=BₜBₜᵀ. Maintain b∈ℤⁿ with Σb=0 and polynomially bounded entries. In addition to edge updates, allow b←b+δ(eₐ−eᵦ), with word-sized δ. Let x=Lₜ†b, f=Bₜᵀx and E=‖f‖₂².

{e: |fₑ|≥ε√E} ⊆ H ⊆ {e: |fₑ|≥(ε/2)√E};   |H|≤4ε⁻².

For E=0 return ∅. Target P,S=Õ(n·poly(1/ε)), expected amortized U=polylog n·poly(1/ε), and Q=Õ(ε−2) to report H. Require high-probability correctness over a polynomial-length oblivious sequence. x is not supplied as a query input.
problems.known: Dynamic electrical-flow locators already exist. [BGJLLPS22] §5.4 builds them from specialized vector and Schur-complement state. The quantified component costs are recorded below; this audit has not verified the strongest bound for the complete topology-plus-demand interface. [JKLS25] instead receives the product-query vector explicitly.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Held for a sharper comparison with existing electrical-flow locators.

The old “related locators exist” paragraph was insufficient. The item remains a research lead, not an audited claim that the requested heavy-hitter interface is new.
comments: The gray band is necessary: edges between ε/2 and ε may be included or omitted.
The queried vector x changes globally after a local graph update. Charging only for Bₜᵀx when x is explicitly supplied would omit the central maintenance cost.
Energy-heavy edges and edges carrying a large fraction of the ℓ₁ flow are different outputs.
literature: Bounded-degree dynamic Laplacian system: Õ(n^(11/12)ε⁻⁵) expected amortized operation cost for its approximate potential/energy interface. Not an automatic support-reporting bound.
The SC component has initialization Õ(mβ⁻²ε⁻²), terminal promotion Õ(β⁻²ε⁻²), and terminal-edge update Õ(1). The locator uses additional vector and terminal-state machinery.
Reports heavy entries of Ah with a term Õ(n+ε⁻²‖Ah‖²₂) in its product-query interface; h is supplied. This does not give the cost of obtaining h=L†b.

audit.decision: Held for a sharper comparison with existing electrical-flow locators.
audit.gap: The proposed target is polylogarithmic topology/demand update and Õ(ε⁻²) implicit-flow reporting; no matching frontier is certified.
audit.caution: The old “related locators exist” paragraph was insufficient. The item remains a research lead, not an audited claim that the requested heavy-hitter interface is new.

bounds.label: Compute and scan the implicit flow afresh
bounds.runtime: U=O(1); Q=Õ(n log(1/ε)); P,S=Õ(n).
bounds.scope: On the bounded-degree expander, solve on the zero-sum subspace to sufficiently small relative energy error, then scan all edges. A grey band permits stable classification; constant-factor slack must be reserved.

bounds.label: Related dynamic Laplacian interface
bounds.scope: Bounded-degree graph, approximate potentials/energy with demand updates; does not itself report the unknown heavy-edge support.

problems.title: Maintain a multiplicative spanning-tree count over a long update sequence
problems.question: Can the spanning-tree count of an always-expander be maintained in truly sublinear update time without accuracy deteriorating with the number of updates?
problems.origin: Dynamic counting question sharpened from [LS23] and [LPY25].
problems.significance: The number of spanning trees is a global combinatorial quantity. Expansion supports fast local resistance estimation, but maintaining a globally accurate count over many updates asks for more than estimating one local ratio. A sublinear maintenance theorem would separate repeated counting from static recomputation.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(V,Eₜ) be a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Each operation inserts or deletes one edge. Every resulting graph satisfies max degree ≤ Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ) ≥ φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀, φ₀. The input is not restricted to planar graphs. Vertices need not remain regular.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).

Let τ(Gₜ) be the number of spanning trees. Fix ε∈(0,1/4). Allow preprocessing Õ(n3/2/ε), space Õ(n·poly(1/ε)), and a known horizon T≤nᴷ.

(1−ε)τ(Gₜ) ≤ τ̂ₜ ≤ (1+ε)τ(Gₜ) for every t≤T.

Target expected amortized U=Õ(n1/2·poly(1/ε)) and Q=polylog(n/ε). The value may use a logarithm or mantissa/exponent representation with sufficient precision to meet the multiplicative guarantee. Require simultaneous high-probability correctness for oblivious updates.
problems.known: Static multiplicative counting has an Õ(m+n3/2/ε) expander benchmark [LS23] and a general-graph Õ(m3/2/ε) benchmark [LPY25]. For a unit edge insertion/deletion, the matrix determinant lemma gives τ(G±e)/τ(G)=1±RG(a,b), with resistance evaluated before the update.
problems.verification: B · Sharpened candidate. The cited static algorithms do not provide the requested long-horizon dynamic guarantee. This catalog found no matching theorem; it does not certify an optimal dynamic frontier.
comments: Per-update relative errors can accumulate when multiplied; a fixed-error estimate of every ratio does not prove the displayed guarantee.
Additive O(εn) error in log τ is much weaker than multiplicative (1±ε) error in τ.
The target is a full count estimate, not just the ratio for the most recent update.
literature: Static (1±ε) tree count on an expander in Õ(m+n^(3/2)/ε) time. Rebuilding gives this update cost.
Static general-graph multiplicative tree count in Õ(m^(3/2)/ε) time. No fully dynamic guarantee is claimed.

Landmark-removal expected cost contains a hitting-time factor h(v,T) times the sum of probabilities that sampled walks use v. This is a graph/landmark-dependent bound, not long-horizon relative determinant-error control.

audit.decision: Retained with the actual rebuild cost and an explicit accumulated-error gap.
audit.gap: Improve U=Õ(n^(3/2)/ε) rebuilding to Õ(√n·poly(1/ε)), with relative count error ε over the full horizon.
audit.caution: The determinant identity is exact, but multiplying individually approximate resistance factors can accumulate error. The required simultaneous ε guarantee must be proved, not inferred from a fixed-error index.

bounds.label: Recompute the count after every update
bounds.runtime: P,U=Õ(n^(3/2)/ε); S=polynomial; Q=O(1) words in logarithmic representation.
bounds.scope: The expander static algorithm, with failure budget divided across a known polynomial horizon. No claimed dynamic improvement.

bounds.label: General-graph static comparator
bounds.scope: For m=Θ(n), the same exponent as the expander rebuild benchmark; does not exploit temporal reuse.

problems.title: Maintain a nearly uniform random spanning tree
problems.question: Can a nearly uniform spanning-tree sample be maintained on an always-expander with sublinear update cost and an explicitly specified sampling guarantee?
problems.origin: Exploratory dynamic sampling interface motivated by static spanning-tree/forest sampling [ALOVV20] and expander resistance methods [LS23].
problems.significance: Sampling a tree is a different task from estimating its total count or maintaining one arbitrary spanning tree. A useful dynamic sampling theorem must specify the distribution at each time and account for the cost of representing a changing tree.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(V,Eₜ) be a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Each operation inserts or deletes one edge. Every resulting graph satisfies max degree ≤ Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ) ≥ φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀, φ₀. The input is not restricted to planar graphs. Vertices need not remain regular.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).

Fix an oblivious sequence of at most nᴷ edge updates. At each time t maintain an implicit spanning tree Tₜ of the current graph. Set η=n−c for a fixed c>0.

dTV(Law(Tₜ), UST(Gₜ)) ≤ η for every t.

Seek expected preprocessing Õ(n), space Õ(n), and amortized update Õ(√n), with O(log n) membership queries “is e in Tₜ?”. Enumerating all tree edges may cost O(n). If changed tree edges are reported after an update, charge their number separately. Samples across times may be correlated; independence is not required.
problems.known: [ALOVV20] Theorem 2 samples within total variation η in O(m log m log(m/η)) time; the paper uses n for the number of edges. Thus m=Θ(n), η=n⁻ᶜ gives O(n log²n) rebuilding per update. A dynamic result must reuse the sample while maintaining its law; merely repairing a spanning tree is insufficient.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Numerical sampling baseline added; novelty remains provisional.

A rapid mixing bound for a fixed chain is not a bound for a chain whose stationary distribution changes after every graph update. No dynamic coupling theorem with the target costs was verified.
comments: The guarantee is a marginal law at each t for a fixed update sequence, not a fresh independent sample on every query.
A random walk tree or an arbitrary maintained spanning tree is not automatically uniform.
Dynamic recourse and mixing under graph changes are part of the statement, not free consequences of static mixing.
literature: A sample within total variation η of the uniform spanning-tree law takes O(m log m log(m/η)) time. For m=Θ(n), η=n⁻ᶜ this is O(n log²n). Static, not dynamic.

problems.title: Beat the square-root update scale for deterministic maximal matching on dense expanders
problems.question: Does constant conductance and linear minimum degree permit deterministic maximal matching with an update exponent strictly below one half?
problems.origin: Updated against the 2026 general-graph result [CKS26], not just the older [BBKS25] baseline.
problems.significance: Dense graphs prevent the trivial bounded-degree repair algorithm from solving the question. The expansion promise may provide a real structural advantage over the current general-graph deterministic bound. The question asks for a strict polynomial saving, not a renamed existing square-root-scale result.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ be a simple unweighted undirected graph on n fixed vertices. Every single-edge insertion/deletion preserves Φ(Gₜ)≥φ₀ and minimum degree ≥cn, for fixed c,φ₀>0; maximum degree is at most n−1. Nonplanar graphs are allowed and no planar restriction is imposed.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).
Maintain Mₜ⊆Eₜ, a matching such that every edge of Gₜ has an endpoint incident to Mₜ.

Seek a deterministic data structure with polynomial preprocessing, O(n² polylog n) space, O(1) mate queries, and amortized U=Õ(n1/2−δ) for some fixed δ>0, against adaptive legal updates.
problems.known: [BBKS25] achieves Õ(n8/9) deterministic amortized update time on general graphs. [CKS26] improves this to n1/2+o(1). Thus merely obtaining an n1/2+o(1) result under expansion is already subsumed.
problems.verification: B · Sharpened candidate. The checked 2026 result does not give an exponent below 1/2. No expander-specific theorem meeting the displayed target was found. Density, determinism and the strict exponent saving are all essential to the claimed gap.

For constant maximum degree, deterministic O(Δ) local repair is elementary, so that setting is excluded.
Oblivious-adversary randomized polylogarithmic algorithms do not answer this deterministic question.
literature: Deterministic fully dynamic maximal matching U=Õ(n^(8/9)); adaptive randomized variant U=Õ(n^(3/4)). The later 2026 deterministic exponent is smaller.
Deterministic fully dynamic maximal matching in n^(1/2+o(1)) amortized update time; a stored mate array answers queries in O(1).

audit.decision: Retained with the May 2026 benchmark.
audit.gap: Improve the deterministic n^(1/2+o(1)) amortized-update benchmark by a fixed polynomial factor under the dense-expander promise.
audit.caution: Bounded-degree maximal matching is easy by local repair; this record intentionally uses dense graphs and must not inherit the degree bound of DG01.

bounds.label: Current verified general-graph benchmark
bounds.runtime: U=n^(1/2+o(1)) amortized; mate query O(1).
bounds.scope: Deterministic fully dynamic maximal matching; dense graphs are allowed.

bounds.label: Previous deterministic bound
bounds.runtime: U=Õ(n^(8/9)); randomized adaptive variant Õ(n^(3/4)).
bounds.scope: General graphs; superseded for the deterministic exponent by the 2026 result.

problems.title: Maintain a perfect matching under robust Hall expansion
problems.question: Can exact perfect matching be maintained in polylogarithmic time when every updated bipartite graph has robust two-sided Hall expansion?
problems.origin: A stronger input promise sharpened from expander matching hardness [HPS22] and online matching in expanders [BZ22].
problems.significance: Ordinary expansion alone does not isolate how much matching slack is available. A robust Hall promise specifies that slack directly and makes existence of a perfect matching automatic. The research question is the cost of maintaining a witness after an edge changes.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(L∪R,Eₜ), |L|=|R|=k, n=2k. Graphs are simple, undirected, unweighted, of maximum degree Δ₀ and conductance at least φ₀. Every individual edge update preserves these conditions and the following promise, for a fixed α>0:

|Nₜ(S)| ≥ (1+α)|S|   for S⊆L or S⊆R, 1≤|S|≤k/2.

Maintain a perfect matching Mₜ, answering mate(v) in O(1). Seek deterministic amortized polylog n update time, Õ(n) space and polynomial preprocessing, against adaptive legal updates. The two-sided promise implies Hall’s condition also for larger subsets.
problems.known: A direct exact baseline finds a new augmenting path after a matched-edge deletion in O(m)=O(n) time. [HPS22] studies hard expander instances, but ordinary expansion must not be identified with this robust Hall promise. [BZ22] uses a static underlying graph and a different online request model.
problems.verification: B · Sharpened candidate; model-sensitive. No quoted source asserts this precise polylogarithmic conjecture. Neither the cited online theorem nor the cited general expander hardness closes the stronger-promise, edge-update formulation as checked here.
comments: The promise is on both bipartition sides; one-sided small-set expansion is not the statement above.
Replacing edge updates by activation/deactivation of left vertices changes the problem.
An approximate matching or a decision that a perfect matching exists does not supply the required exact mate queries.
literature: For exact maximum matching / perfect-matching existence on constant-degree constant-expansion general graphs, OMv excludes U=O(n^(1/2−δ)) and Q=O(n^(1−δ)). The construction is nonbipartite and does not satisfy this robust-Hall promise.

Theorem 1.2: lossless expansion (2D/3+2) up to K allows O(log N) load and O(D log N) bit operations per request/retraction, or O(D) on a log N-bit word RAM. Static edges; not load-one dynamic perfect matching.

audit.decision: Retained; the robust Hall promise is part of the problem, not an inferred property of expanders.
audit.gap: Improve a deterministic O(n)-time augmenting-path repair after a matched-edge deletion to polylog n.
audit.caution: Ordinary conductance does not imply the two-sided (1+α) Hall promise. A hardness transfer or positive theorem must verify it after every intermediate edge update.

bounds.label: Exact dynamic repair
bounds.runtime: P=polynomial; S=O(n); U=O(n) worst-case; mate query O(1).
bounds.scope: Insertion leaves the current perfect matching valid. One matched-edge deletion requires one augmenting path; m=O(n).

bounds.label: Related online matching result
bounds.runtime: O(D) word operations per request/retraction; load O(log N).
bounds.scope: Lossless expansion at least 2D/3+2 up to K, static underlying edges. Both the allowed load and update primitive differ.

problems.title: Near-exact s–t max-flow / min-cut values on capacitated expanders
problems.question: Can arbitrary s–t queries on a capacitated always-expander be answered within a (1+ε) factor in Õ(√n) time with polylogarithmic updates?
problems.formulation:
Gₜ=(V,Eₜ,cₜ) is a simple undirected capacitated graph on n fixed vertices, with mₜ≤M=O(n log²n). Every nonzero capacity is an integer in [1,nᴷ], for a fixed K. An update inserts or deletes one edge, or changes one capacity. All states satisfy capacity-weighted conductance Φc(Gₜ)≥φ₀ for a fixed 0<φ₀≤1/4. There is no degree bound and no planar restriction. M is known; the initial graph is explicit.

Φc(G)=min∅≠S⊊V c(∂S)/min{volc(S),volc(V∖S)},   volc(S)=Σv∈SΣe∋vc(e).
λₜ(s,t)=mins∈S, t∉Scₜ(∂S)=max{F: Bf=F(eₛ−eₜ), |fₑ|≤cₜ(e)}.

Queries require s≠t. B is a vertex-by-edge incidence matrix for an arbitrary fixed orientation; f is signed and F≥0 is its s–t flow value.

Fix ε∈(0,1/10). Query(s,t) returns λ̂ with λ/(1+ε)≤λ̂≤λ. Seek P=Õ(M·poly(1/ε)), S=Õ(M·poly(1/ε)), expected amortized U=polylog n·poly(1/ε), and worst-case Q=Õ(√n·poly(1/ε)). Require simultaneous high-probability correctness for every query in a polynomial-length oblivious sequence. Only a scalar value is requested; neither a cut partition nor a feasible flow is included.
problems.significance: This isolates whether expansion enables accurate many-pair flow queries without a graph-wide max-flow computation per query. The approximation parameter must be stated: a generic constant-factor estimate is already elementary on a constant-conductance graph.
problems.known: The endpoint-degree estimate below is constant-factor but not (1+ε). Static approximate max-flow gives an Õ(M/ε) query baseline. Dynamic tree-flow approximations give different approximation/update tradeoffs; they do not establish this precision and query cost.
comments: Capacity-weighted expansion is required. Expansion of only the unweighted support would allow tiny-capacity edges to mask flow bottlenecks.
The graph is sparse but capacities and vertex degrees may grow. The bounded-degree unit-capacity local enumeration does not apply.
Reporting a feasible flow is a separate interface: an explicit edge vector may need Ω(m) output time.
literature: Static time O(m log⁹n log log n+ε⁻¹m log⁶n) for (1−ε)-approximate undirected max-flow. Recomputing per query gives Õ(M/ε).
Fully dynamic nearly-logarithmic-factor all-pair flow/cut approximation: Õ(n^(2/3)) amortized operations, oblivious adversary; Õ(m^(3/4)) adaptive variant. The approximation is not 1+ε.
Unweighted deterministic dynamic flow/min-cut value estimates with n^o(1) approximation and worst-case update time, Q=O(log^(1/6)n). Related model, not a near-exact weighted result.
Unweighted exact Gomory–Hu tree in n^(3/2+o(1)) worst-case update time. Does not directly cover arbitrary capacities.

problems.title: Report maximum flows using logarithmic total path length
problems.question: Can an always-expander report a maximum s–t flow as edge-disjoint paths of O(log n) total length, with polylogarithmic updates and queries?
problems.formulation:
Gₜ is a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Every edge insertion or deletion preserves maximum degree Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ)≥φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀,φ₀. The class has no planar restriction; expansion is promised, not certified by the data structure.

Φ(G)=min∅≠S⊊V |∂S| / min{vol(S),vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈Sdeg(v).
λₜ(s,t)=mins∈S, t∉Scₜ(∂S)=max{F: Bf=F(eₛ−eₜ), |fₑ|≤cₜ(e)}.

Queries require s≠t. B is a vertex-by-edge incidence matrix for an arbitrary fixed orientation; f is signed and F≥0 is its s–t flow value.

Here c(e)=1. For arbitrary queried s,t, return λₜ(s,t) pairwise edge-disjoint simple s–t paths. Let L be their total number of reported edges. Seek deterministic P,S=n^(1+o(1)), amortized U=polylog n, and worst-case Q=polylog n+O(L) over polynomial-length adaptive legal sequences. Require L≤K₀ log n for a constant K₀ depending only on Δ₀ and φ₀. No full n-bit cut partition is requested. The feasibility argument below is part of the baseline audit, so the length condition is not an unsupported assumption.
problems.significance: Even when an exact min-cut value can be found locally, constructing the global routes that realize it is a different task. This question explicitly asks for a feasible maximum flow, rather than reusing a scalar min-cut theorem as a path-reporting claim.
problems.known: At most Δ₀ integral augmentations suffice. In a unit-capacity residual graph carrying value F≤Δ₀, every directed cut has residual capacity at least |∂S|−F. For |S|≤n/2 this is at least φ₀|S|−F. If an augmenting path exists, a forward or backward BFS ball gains at least one vertex per layer until size 2F/φ₀, then grows geometrically (degree is bounded and each residual capacity is at most two). The two balls meet after O(log n) layers. Consequently shortest augmentations produce a maximum flow whose total support length is O(Δ₀ log n)=O(log n); removing circulations and decomposing it preserves this bound. Fresh computation still scans O(n) edges in the worst case. This is an elementary feasibility/baseline argument, not the requested fast data structure.
comments: The scalar value and a small minimum-cut side are already computable in constant time for fixed Δ₀,φ₀ by the local enumeration in the audit note. That solved variant is not the open question.
The total-length requirement L≤K₀ log n prevents a long, otherwise valid witness from absorbing a linear query cost. K₀ is independent of n.
For a fixed s,t maintained permanently, the problem changes: the index may be specialized to that pair. This record requires arbitrary query pairs.

This is stronger than DG02: returning one constituent path gives a short s–t path. The extra requirement is maximum flow value and simultaneous edge-disjointness, not merely several independently found paths.
literature: For c=(log n)^o(1), deterministic fully dynamic threshold connectivity has n^o(1) worst-case update and query time. It does not by itself provide output-linear maximum-flow path reporting.
For any fixed α>0, U=O(n^α) supports constant-stretch single-path reporting. A single short path is not a collection of λ edge-disjoint paths.
Unweighted exact all-pair cut values represented by a maintained Gomory–Hu tree, U=n^(3/2+o(1)). A cut tree is not an explicit feasible flow in the input graph.
problems.origin: A newly specified query interface synthesized from the primary results in the literature table. The target is proposed here, not quoted as an author conjecture.
problems.verification: The scalar min-cut variant is elementary in this class and is excluded. The witness question includes an n-independent logarithmic total-length guarantee, justified above. The audit separates this existence bound from the unresolved update/query interface, and does not identify directed residual graphs with undirected expanders.

audit.decision: Added as a witness problem; the scalar variant is excluded.
audit.gap: Reduce O(n) fresh computation to polylogarithmic query time while keeping total reported length O(log n), with polylogarithmic updates.
audit.caution: The logarithmic witness length has an elementary residual-cut justification, but a fast maintained reporting interface was not verified. A directed residual graph is not automatically covered by an undirected expander path oracle.

bounds.runtime: P,S=O(n); U=O(1); Q=O(Δ₀m)=O(n); total reported length L=O(log n).
bounds.scope: Use shortest residual augmenting paths, at most Δ₀ times. The residual-cut growth argument in Known results bounds each path length; cancel circulations and decompose the final integral flow.

bounds.scope: Enumerate connected sets of size ≤⌊Δ₀/φ₀⌋ rooted at s or t; the proof is in the excluded-variants audit. Does not produce global flow paths.

problems.question: Can exact arbitrary-pair cut values on sparse capacitated always-expanders have Õ(√n) updates and polylogarithmic queries?
problems.formulation:
Gₜ=(V,Eₜ,cₜ) is a simple undirected capacitated graph on n fixed vertices, with mₜ≤M=O(n log²n). Every nonzero capacity is an integer in [1,nᴷ], for a fixed K. An update inserts or deletes one edge, or changes one capacity. All states satisfy capacity-weighted conductance Φc(Gₜ)≥φ₀ for a fixed 0<φ₀≤1/4. There is no degree bound and no planar restriction. M is known; the initial graph is explicit.

Φc(G)=min∅≠S⊊V c(∂S)/min{volc(S),volc(V∖S)},   volc(S)=Σv∈SΣe∋vc(e).
λₜ(s,t)=mins∈S, t∉Scₜ(∂S)=max{F: Bf=F(eₛ−eₜ), |fₑ|≤cₜ(e)}.

Queries require s≠t. B is a vertex-by-edge incidence matrix for an arbitrary fixed orientation; f is signed and F≥0 is its s–t flow value.

Return the exact integer λₜ(s,t). Target deterministic preprocessing P=M^(1+o(1)), space S=M^(1+o(1)) words, amortized U=Õ(√n), and worst-case Q=polylog n for arbitrary polynomial-length legal sequences. Arithmetic uses Θ(log n)-bit words, with the constant depending on K. The query returns a value only. The integer capacity bound is essential and is not expanded into unit parallel edges.
problems.significance: This separates exactness from the fixed-relative-error problem. The input size remains almost linear, while cut values can be polynomially large; exact small-connectivity routines no longer cover all queries.
problems.known: Theorem 4.7 of [KK26] records a deterministic M^(1+o(1))-time static Gomory–Hu construction even for polynomially weighted graphs. The O(1/φ₀) endpoint-degree estimate is again trivial but not exact. Graphs with a fixed maximum weighted degree would fall into a different parameter regime.
Maintaining a Gomory–Hu tree is stronger than merely answering exact values with this space bound; do not assume a tree representation has small update recourse.

Static weighted Gomory–Hu construction: m^(1+o(1)) deterministic time (Thm. 4.7). Fully dynamic unweighted tree: n^(3/2+o(1)) worst-case update (Thm. 1.5). Distinguish the two models.
Exact threshold c-edge-connectivity for c=(log n)^o(1) in n^o(1) worst-case update/query time. Polynomially large capacities and cut values exceed that regime.

problems.title: Classify ordinary prediction on the two-dimensional von Neumann lattice
problems.question: Is ordinary sandpile prediction on the uniform nearest-neighbor square lattice in NC, P-complete, or of intermediate complexity?
problems.origin: Classical open problem from [MN99]; explicitly organized in [FP20] and still identified as open in [CLP26].
problems.significance: This is a central boundary case for parallel prediction: the geometry permits planar interactions but does not provide the crossover used in higher-dimensional hardness constructions. Resolving the precise standard model would settle a longstanding complexity classification.
problems.formulation:
Use the uniform, unweighted Abelian sandpile on ℤ², with the specified translation-invariant neighborhood ℕ. A site with at least θ=|ℕ| grains sends one grain to each x+a, a∈ℕ, in a firing. Configurations have finite support and are encoded by an explicit finite rectangle with zeros elsewhere. This is the infinite lattice with finite input, not a periodic torus.

ℕ={(1,0),(−1,0),(0,1),(0,−1)}, θ=4.

Input: c(x)∈{0,…,7} on the rectangle and a site q. Let uc(q) denote the total number of firings at q during stabilization.

PREDVN(c,q) = 1 ⇔ uc(q)>0.

Determine membership in uniform NC, or P-completeness under logspace many-one reductions; these are candidate outcomes, not an assumed exhaustive dichotomy. Input size is the explicit rectangle area plus coordinate encoding. Heights are bounded, not exponentially compressed. This record uses the general PRED convention of the 2020 survey.
problems.known: [MN99] separates one-dimensional tractability from hardness in dimensions at least three. The survey [FP20] leaves the two-dimensional case open. Recent changes of weights or local rules [CLP26] address different models.
problems.verification: A · Source-explicit open problem. The 2020 survey’s Open Question 4 and the June 2026 preprint were checked. No closure of the uniform von Neumann problem was located through 2026-09-08.
comments: Single-grain avalanche prediction is a related restricted input problem, not automatically an equivalent definition.
No crossover of a specified kind does not imply an NC algorithm.
P-completeness is a statement about parallel complexity; it does not establish a quadratic sequential-time lower bound.
literature: Prediction in d≥3 is P-complete; a one-dimensional version lies in NC³. These are dimension-dependent classifications, not an algorithm for the uniform two-dimensional case.
Bounded-height explicit-input prediction is in P. Proposition 6 gives first-column ≤AC⁰ single-addition ≤AC⁰ general prediction; Open Question 4 includes the uniform 2D von Neumann and Moore gaps.
Weighted/nonuniform crossing gates are constructed; the classical uniform 2D von Neumann/Moore classification remains unresolved. No uniform-model runtime improvement is supplied.
Arbitrary Boolean circuits can be embedded for the stated fungal update model. This is a rule-specific hardness result, not a uniform 2D Abelian-sandpile runtime bound.

problems.title: Near-linear exact stabilization on a random regular graph
problems.question: Does random regular topology permit near-linear exact stabilization for an arbitrary graph-independent initial configuration?
problems.origin: Exploratory distributional restriction of the expander stabilization gap in [CC24].
problems.significance: A worst-case expander may hide local structure that makes integer stabilization expensive. Random topology provides a separate, testable input model. Requiring initial heights to be independent of the sampled graph prevents the average-case promise from silently reverting to an adaptive worst-case instance.
problems.formulation:
Input: a connected simple undirected graph G on n vertices, an absorbing sink s, and σ:V∖{s}→ℕ, given explicitly in binary, with N=Σσ(v)≤nᴷ for a fixed K. A nonsink v fires when it has at least degG(v) grains, sending one grain along every incident edge; grains reaching s disappear. Let u(v) count all legal firings and σ° be the unique stable configuration.

Fix d≥3, a label s, and a configuration σ on the remaining labels, before sampling G uniformly from simple d-regular graphs on n labeled vertices (nd even), conditioned on Φ(G)≥φ₀ for a suitable fixed φ₀>0. σ is not sampled from a recurrent sandpile measure.

σ° = σ − Lsu,   u∈ℕn−1,   0≤σ°(v)<degG(v).

Seek an always-correct algorithm whose runtime is Õ(n) with probability ≥1−n−c, for some fixed c>0, over G and internal randomness, for every such fixed σ with N≤nᴷ. Permit a slower exact fallback. State space usage, with Õ(n) as the target.
problems.known: The checked general expander stabilization bound [CC24] does not specialize to near-linear time merely from its displayed parameters. Random regularity offers a stronger input distribution, not an already-proved improvement.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Distributional question retained as provisional.

The probability space, conditioning and independence of the initial configuration are explicit; no average-case runtime theorem matching the target was verified.
comments: High probability concerns runtime; correctness remains exact on every sampled instance.
An initial configuration chosen after inspecting G is outside this statement.
Stationary avalanche statistics and computational complexity for an explicitly given σ are different tasks.

Spectral-gap/conductance relations yield O(log n) mixing/diameter scales for fixed-gap bounded-degree expanders. Background theorem, not a dynamic-update or exact sandpile algorithm.

problems.title: A compact index for independent avalanche queries
problems.question: Can all single-grain firing queries on a fixed expander background be answered quickly from a near-linear-size index?
problems.origin: Exploratory preprocessing interface combining ordinary avalanche prediction [FP20] with exact finite-graph stabilization [CC24].
problems.significance: A single fixed graph and background may be queried many times. An n-by-n truth table answers immediately but hides quadratic storage. A compact index would identify compressible structure in the complete avalanche-response relation.
problems.formulation:
Input for preprocessing: a simple undirected unweighted n-vertex graph G with maximum degree Δ₀, conductance at least φ₀, one absorbing sink s, and a fixed stable background σ with 0≤σ(v)<deg(v). All are explicit. Every query is an independent experiment starting from that same σ.

query(p,q)=1 ⇔ uσ+eₚ(q)>0,   p,q≠s.

Seek deterministic polynomial preprocessing, space Õ(n) words and worst-case polylog n query time. Stabilization uses threshold degG(v) and absorption at s. The preprocessing may depend on both G and σ; neither changes. The query does not advance a physical sandpile state.
problems.known: Precomputing all n−1 possible additions with a static solver gives a polynomial-preprocessing, O(n²)-bit table and O(1) queries. The proposed gain is space with retained fast queries, not a new way to obtain polynomial preprocessing.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Space/query tradeoff made explicit; novelty provisional.

No matching compact index or space lower bound was verified. This is a tradeoff question, not evidence that a polylogarithmic query is intrinsically hard.
comments: The task reports one Boolean firing event, not all final heights.
Independent queries reset to σ; online additions would define a different data structure.
The sink and stable background are part of the preprocessed input, so they cannot be varied for free.
literature: Bounded-height explicit-input prediction is in P. Proposition 6 gives first-column ≤AC⁰ single-addition ≤AC⁰ general prediction; Open Question 4 includes the uniform 2D von Neumann and Moore gaps.
Exact algorithms: trees O(n log n), pseudotrees O(n log²n), paths/cliques O(n). General bound O(Rm² log(nN)) counts batch iterations; per-iteration work must also be charged.

problems.title: Output-sensitive processing of online grain additions
problems.question: Can an online sequence of grain additions be processed in time proportional to the number of changed coordinates, rather than the number of toppling events?
problems.origin: Exploratory online extension of exact finite-graph prediction [CC24].
problems.significance: An avalanche may topple the same site many times. Recording the odometer once per affected site can be far smaller than replaying every event. A data structure with this output measure would support repeated exact simulation without demanding an impossible constant-time full-state output.
problems.formulation:
Fix a simple unweighted undirected graph G with n vertices, max degree Δ₀, Φ(G)≥φ₀ and an absorbing sink s. Start from an explicitly given stable σ₀. Receive an arbitrary online sequence p₁,p₂,… of nonsink vertices, of length at most nᴷ.

σₜ = stabilizeG,s(σₜ₋₁+eₚₜ);   uₜ = the odometer of this addition.

After each addition report every vertex in Aₜ={v:uₜ(v)>0 or σₜ(v)≠σₜ₋₁(v)}, together with uₜ(v) and σₜ(v). Let kₜ=|Aₜ|. Target Õ(n) preprocessing/space and deterministic amortized Õ(1+kₜ) time per operation. Count the addition vertex even when no site fires and only its height changes.
problems.known: Event simulation pays for individual firings, while a static exact solver recomputes a whole stabilization. Neither bound automatically gives the proposed coordinate-sensitive online cost.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Output measure retained; temporal-reuse frontier provisional.

Near-linear work per avalanche, if known, would still differ from Õ(1+k) for small avalanches. No theorem establishing this exact output-sensitive dynamic guarantee was verified.
comments: kₜ counts distinct affected coordinates; Σᵥuₜ(v) counts events and may be much larger.
The topology is fixed. Edge insertion/deletion would change thresholds and defines a separate problem.
The state persists between operations, unlike the independent-query index.
literature: Exact algorithms: trees O(n log n), pseudotrees O(n log²n), paths/cliques O(n). General bound O(Rm² log(nN)) counts batch iterations; per-iteration work must also be charged.
Least action characterizes the legal odometer as a minimal nonnegative stabilizing firing vector. Structural result; no fast-algorithm bound is asserted.

audit.decision: Output measure retained; temporal-reuse frontier provisional.
audit.gap: Reduce Õ(n²) recomputation per addition to Õ(1+k), where k is the number of affected coordinates.
audit.caution: Near-linear work per avalanche, if known, would still differ from Õ(1+k) for small avalanches. No theorem establishing this exact output-sensitive dynamic guarantee was verified.

problems.title: Exact sandpile queries under expander-preserving edge updates
problems.question: Can exact stabilization queries for a fixed initial configuration be maintained as the underlying graph changes but always remains an expander?
problems.origin: Exploratory intersection of dynamic expander problems and finite-graph sandpile prediction [CC24].
problems.significance: This formulation makes the overlap between the two requested domains explicit. A local edge change alters both transport and firing thresholds, and can change the exact legal odometer globally. The question is whether coordinate queries can avoid repeating a full stabilization.
problems.formulation:
Let Gₜ=(V,Eₜ) be a simple, undirected, unweighted graph on n fixed vertices. Each operation inserts or deletes one edge. Every resulting graph satisfies max degree ≤ Δ₀ and conductance Φ(Gₜ) ≥ φ₀, for fixed positive constants Δ₀, φ₀. The input is not restricted to planar graphs. Vertices need not remain regular.

Φ(G) = min∅≠S⊊V |E(S,V∖S)| / min{vol(S), vol(V∖S)},   vol(S)=Σv∈S deg(v).

Fix a sink s∈V and one original configuration σ:V∖{s}→ℕ with total N≤nᴷ. At every time t, independently stabilize this same original σ on Gₜ with sink s and thresholds degGₜ(v). Let the resulting odometer and stable state be uₜ and σₜ°. Heights are not carried over from the preceding graph.

query(v) returns (uₜ(v), σₜ°(v)) exactly;   σₜ° = σ − Lₜ,suₜ.

Seek deterministic polynomial preprocessing, Õ(n²) space, amortized U=Õ(n1−δ) for some fixed δ>0, and worst-case Q=polylog n, for arbitrary polynomial-length legal updates. The target is an index, not materializing every changed coordinate after each edge update.
problems.known: Recomputing from scratch after each update is a static-solver baseline. An approximate dynamic Laplacian solver [DGGP19] does not enforce the integer legality and stability conditions that define the exact answer.
problems.verification:
On hold as a paper-selection claim. Exploratory interface retained with a concrete fallback.

Approximate dynamic Laplacian solvers do not automatically respect legal integer stabilization. No directly matching dynamic sandpile theorem or lower bound was verified.
comments: The same original σ is reinterpreted on each graph; this is a deterministic function of (Gₜ,σ), not a physical sandpile with changing infrastructure.
Both degrees and the grounded Laplacian change. Treating an edge update as a demand update alone is incorrect.
Exact point queries avoid the unavoidable cost of reporting a potentially global state change, but must still reflect legal stabilization.
literature: Exact algorithms: trees O(n log n), pseudotrees O(n log²n), paths/cliques O(n). General bound O(Rm² log(nN)) counts batch iterations; per-iteration work must also be charged.
Related dynamic linear-algebra interface; approximation does not solve the integer problem.
Least action characterizes the legal odometer as a minimal nonnegative stabilizing firing vector. Structural result; no fast-algorithm bound is asserted.

audit.decision: Exploratory interface retained with a concrete fallback.
audit.gap: Reduce Õ(n²) fresh stabilization after a topology change to sublinear U while retaining exact coordinate queries.
audit.caution: Approximate dynamic Laplacian solvers do not automatically respect legal integer stabilization. No directly matching dynamic sandpile theorem or lower bound was verified.

auditProtocol: Freeze the interface: graph family, expansion measure, degree/capacity range, input encoding, output, adversary, lifetime and all quantifiers.
Identify the strongest directly comparable result verified in the search. Record numerical costs and the theorem location. Separate different models and elementary baselines.
Substitute the parameters of the proposed setting. Charge preprocessing, epoch rebuilding, output size, recourse and failure probability over the full sequence.
Check triviality and already-solved variants. Test whether a cited reduction preserves every graph promise and whether its gap survives the requested approximation.
State one precise remaining gap. Source-explicit openness, an independently formulated candidate and an incompletely audited lead receive different visible statuses.
Check later primary work and record the search boundary. A failed search is not evidence of impossibility, nor a proof that a question is open.

exclusions.title: Exact s–t cut value on unit-capacity constant-degree, constant-conductance graphs is not a new open problem.
exclusions.proof: Let λ=λ(s,t)≤Δ₀. A minimum s–t cut can be chosen with both sides connected: any component containing neither terminal could be moved to the other side and strictly decrease the positive-capacity cut. Let A be its smaller-volume side. Expansion gives vol(A)≤λ/φ₀≤Δ₀/φ₀; connectivity of G gives |A|≤vol(A). Thus A is a connected set of at most ⌊Δ₀/φ₀⌋ vertices containing s or t. Enumerate connected sets of this size rooted at the two terminals, discard sets containing both, and minimize boundary size. There are Δ₀^O(Δ₀/φ₀) candidates and the same constant-parameter work suffices to return A and its cut edges. Maintain adjacency in O(1) per legal update. This establishes a value/small-cut oracle, not an oracle that reports maximum-flow paths.

exclusions.title: A constant-factor capacitated flow-value estimate is also elementary.
exclusions.proof: For d=min{volc(s),volc(t)}, every separating cut has both side-volumes at least d. Consequently φ₀d≤λ(s,t)≤d. Maintaining weighted degrees yields a 1/φ₀ approximation in O(1) query time. DG10 requires 1+ε; DG12 requires the exact integer value.

exclusions.title: Short-cycle hardness is not established for DG02.
exclusions.proof: The catalog has not verified a reduction from a named conjecture or a precise short-cycle benchmark to this promised dynamic interface. Deleting already extracted cycles can destroy conductance. The static cycle-decomposition literature therefore provides related algorithmic context, not a hardness certificate.

exclusions.title: Other excluded variants.
exclusions.proof: Promised connectivity; bounded-degree maximal matching; deletion-only diameter-bounded path maintenance; fixed-error resistance estimation without additional requirements; exact tree/pseudotree stabilization already covered by CC24; ordinary crossover nonexistence already proved for full Moore.
